items.title: Google mandates AI agents to use Workspace MCP servers from February 2027, restricting Gmail API email sending to partners [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Google announced that starting February 1, 2027, all AI-driven tools accessing Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and other Workspace services must use its MCP servers. The new policy restricts certain Gmail API functions like sending, replying, and forwarding emails to partner-approved tools, limiting independent developers to draft creation only. This change affects AI assistants and agents that interact with Workspace APIs, requiring them to comply with updated terms or face access restrictions. The Workspace AI Tools Addendum also imposes data processing limits, including a 30-day cap on retention of technical information like vector embeddings and memory indexes, and bans on using Workspace data for training or building competing products. While Docs, Slides, and Tasks APIs have near-complete coverage on MCP servers, Gmail and Drive have significant functional gaps. Google has not clarified partner access criteria or timelines for broader availability of restricted features, creating disparities between large AI vendors and independent developers. Google's definitions of AI agents are broad, encompassing personal scripts and third-party services, with self-declaration required via OAuth client settings. Non-compliant agents calling REST APIs directly will face standard-tier quotas and potential policy violations. The policy aims to regulate AI agent access to Workspace data while maintaining control over sensitive operations and data usage.

items.title: Researchers propose a background-independent algebraic quantization of vacuum general relativity using null cones, deriving finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and recovering black hole entropy corrections
items.content_text: Researchers propose a background-independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four-dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes by solving gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones and promoting canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations. They construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation and obtain a Lorentzian path integral with absolutely convergent sums over intermediate states, computing finite graviton pair creation amplitudes nonperturbatively in Newton's constant. The approach uses diffeomorphism invariance to show that macroscopic causal diamonds have finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and derives the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy with logarithmic corrections for large Schwarzschild black holes, matching previous Euclidean results. The theory also recovers the semiclassical Einstein equations at one loop as its low-energy limit, providing a novel algebraic framework for quantum gravity.

items.title: Nature reports AI labs may have found algorithms that could break Internet public-key encryption in polynomial time, potentially undermining RSA security [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A recent Nature essay discusses unconfirmed reports that leading AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, may have discovered algorithms capable of breaking public-key cryptography like RSA in polynomial time, which would challenge the mathematical foundations of Internet security. These claims, while not yet verified, have sparked concern among computer scientists about the future of encrypted communications. The essay explains that such algorithms could theoretically solve problems previously considered intractable, but practical application might still be limited by computational complexity. Researchers remain cautious, noting that while this could signal a major shift, the longstanding P vs NP question remains unresolved, and some recent AI-driven mathematical advances suggest many cryptographic problems may still be hard to solve. The article explores the implications for data protection and the ongoing efforts to safeguard Internet security against emerging AI capabilities.

items.title: Q.ANT develops photonic processors using light waves to run AI models with lower energy consumption, piloting chips in IONOS data centers [ * ] [ ◼ ]

These chips are designed to complement GPUs by handling tasks like image recognition and robotics more efficiently, potentially cutting energy use by four to five times under simulation. Q.ANT has deployed its photonic chips in a pilot program with cloud provider IONOS, where over 30 engineering teams are developing AI models optimized for this technology. The company emphasizes that photonic processors are not intended to replace GPUs but to work alongside them, leveraging light's wave properties to execute complex math in fewer steps and with less cooling required, addressing key data center cost drivers.

items.title: Developer open-sources Ghost Mode Rust library to reduce token usage by about 60% in AI agents through in-process code execution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A developer has released Ghost Mode, a Rust library that implements a Code Mode for AI agents to reduce token consumption by allowing the model to execute chained tool calls via short Python scripts within the process. This approach avoids sending intermediate results back to the model, significantly lowering token usage and API costs compared to traditional tool calls. Ghost Mode runs scripts inside the host process using Rust function calls, enabling the model to handle complex workflows with fewer tokens and steps. The library supports sandboxing and offers features for secure script execution, aiming to improve efficiency and reduce billing for AI applications that interact with multiple tools or APIs.

items.title: Developer says AI is eroding coding skills but does not mind as skills evolve and new tools enable building projects previously out of reach [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A developer reflects on a survey showing 63% of heavy AI users feel their coding skills are diminishing but expresses no concern, viewing this as part of the natural evolution of programming skills. The author notes that while their manual coding ability, especially in JavaScript, has declined, they continue to build complex applications using AI tools and new languages they cannot write by hand. The article discusses how coding skills have always changed with technology, comparing current AI reliance to past shifts like Internet Explorer workarounds becoming obsolete. The author emphasizes that some skills, such as debugging and directing AI agents, remain important. They also highlight that pressure to produce more with AI correlates with feeling skill loss and reduced enjoyment, but working independently without such pressure mitigates these effects. The author advises developers to focus on building projects they previously could not due to skill or time constraints, suggesting that while traditional coding skills may fade, the ability to deliver products and direct AI tools is becoming more valuable. They also note that learning to code remains essential for a software engineering career but may be less critical for product creators leveraging AI.

The setup demonstrated the ability to identify most historical bugs in tests and returns reviews within minutes, integrating with continuous integration systems to escalate complex cases to human reviewers. The decision followed an evaluation of 75 open-source code review tools, narrowing down to 20 credible options based on criteria such as open-source availability, multi-model support, and practical effectiveness. Strumenta prioritized a solution that balances quality, speed, and cost, and allows flexibility to switch models as technology evolves. This approach addresses the growing bottleneck in code review caused by increased code production with AI-assisted development tools. By adopting this incremental improvement to their development process, Strumenta aims to maintain code quality without overwhelming human reviewers, reflecting a pragmatic shift toward integrating AI tools in software engineering workflows while preserving human oversight where necessary.

items.title: Qubes OS runs local AI inference using an unlocked NVIDIA RTX 5080 Blackwell GPU and integrated GPU SR-IOV for secure multi-qube acceleration [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A demonstration shows a production laptop running local AI inference on Qubes OS by passing through an NVIDIA RTX 5080 Laptop GPU based on Blackwell architecture to a dedicated inference qube. The setup overcomes device initialization errors by disabling integrated graphics at boot and reconstructs power management inside the guest to raise the GPU power ceiling from 80 W to 175 W, achieving around 3,700 tokens per second throughput. To maintain system acceleration for other qubes, the integrated Arrow Lake GPU uses SR-IOV to provide one physical and seven virtual functions assignable to work qubes. This configuration enables two GPUs with different sharing models on a single machine, delivering inference services to all qubes over qrexec without network exposure, preserving Qubes OS's compartmentalization security model.

items.title: MIT CSAIL and Harvard researchers develop LARS method to reduce memory usage by up to 47% when fine-tuning AI models on small devices [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers at MIT CSAIL and Harvard have created the Low-memory Activation Rank Subspace (LARS) method to make fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) more memory-efficient on devices with limited resources, such as smartphones and wearables. LARS reduces the memory footprint by summarizing intermediate activation data during training, cutting memory use by over 23% on GPUs and about 47% on CPUs compared to existing techniques. The team tested LARS on a Raspberry Pi 5 with an 8 GB memory limit, achieving 9% more memory savings than the leading Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method at long context lengths. While LARS slightly trades off accuracy for memory efficiency, it significantly lowers energy consumption by roughly 22%, making it a more sustainable approach for on-device AI training. The method can also be combined with other optimization techniques to further reduce memory and energy use.

items.title: Standard Kernel uses AI-driven software optimizations to make Intel Gaudi2 chips outperform Nvidia H100 on long-context inference benchmarks with 60% higher decode throughput [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Standard Kernel demonstrated that software optimizations can significantly improve Intel Gaudi2 AI accelerator performance, achieving 60% higher decode throughput and 9.4 times better cost efficiency than Nvidia's H100 on a long-context inference workload. The improvements were made without hardware changes, focusing on optimizing the entire software stack for the Qwen3.5-27B model. Intel's Gaudi2 chips, originally seen as uncompetitive due to limited software support despite strong hardware specs, were enhanced through techniques such as reducing prefill padding, speeding up attention mechanisms, and optimizing memory usage. These changes allowed Gaudi2 to surpass Nvidia's flagship H100 80GB PCIe accelerator in throughput while costing only 17% of the hourly rental price. This case highlights the critical role of software in unlocking AI hardware potential and suggests a future where heterogeneous AI inference platforms rely heavily on software innovation to maximize performance and cost-effectiveness across diverse architectures.

The discussion covers practical implications including selective automation, active learning, and sensor fusion, highlighting why faithful uncertainty estimates are crucial despite models always being approximations.

The fine-tuning targeted Dell-specific terms and products that the original embedding models struggled to understand, improving search accuracy across internal sources like GitHub, Jira, and Confluence. items.title: How Bankers Are Turning Tech Stock Volatility Into Cash [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Tech firms spending heavily on AI buildouts have flooded the market with new stock sales this year. And with investments in AI infrastructure soaking up so much investor cash, raising money for other capital-hungry areas of tech like quantum computing and robotics is requiring especially creative dealmaking. For companies that are already public but need more cash for ambitious projects, sharp swings in their share prices are making it tough to sell more stock at an attractive price. Bankers say one workaround is turning that volatility into a selling point by bundling shares with warrants, which give investors the right to buy more stock later at a locked-in price. If investors are willing to pay up for a chance at a future payoff, companies can sell stock at a premium rather than the usual discount for new share sales. One recent example is quantum computing company IonQ, which raised $2 billion in mid-October at a 15% premium to its prior closing price. In the IonQ deal, investors got stock plus warrants to buy more shares at double the stock's pre-offering price within the next seven years, an extra way for them to profit if IonQ's stock soars. IonQ has raised $5 billion in total through three such offerings since July 2025, helping pay for an acquisition spree that expanded its business into chip manufacturing and cybersecurity. The company's stock has been volatile over that period, falling sharply from an October 2025 high of $82, rebounding to about $70 this May and then tumbling again. The shares currently trade around $21. With tech investors particularly skittish right now, there's more reason for cash-hungry companies to pounce on any opportunities to raise money. That's also boosting the appeal of at-the-market stock sales, which allow companies to sell shares gradually into the open market, giving them the flexibility to take advantage of rallies. And while less conventional ways of raising equity were once viewed on Wall Street as signs of desperation, bankers say that stigma has faded in recent years as companies have embraced the benefits of having more options for raising cash. "Historically, ATMs and some of these more creative financing tools have been a bit of a scarlet letter...it was hard to get a management team or board around them," said Connor Leahey, managing director at Cohen & Co. Capital Markets. "And now it's totally shifted." But getting to the public market in the first place has also become much tougher. Investors have had to sop up a surge in new stock issued by already-public tech giants this year alongside mega listings from SpaceX and last week's debut by Anthropic, with most of those shares performing poorly after their IPOs. The broader market for tech debuts has all but dried up, and Anthropic's rapid drop below its offering price doesn't bode well for other IPO hopefuls. That helps explain a comparative burst of activity in mergers with special purpose acquisition companies. Five companies went public via a SPAC merger in October, including two space technology firms and a semiconductor tech company, according to data and analytics company Boardroom Alpha. Four more companies have gone public via SPAC so far this month, including robotics company Agility Robotics and spacecraft developer Quantum Space. Public debuts via SPAC boomed in 2020 and 2021 before falling sharply in recent years after a string of poorly performing deals and other market headwinds. But companies and bankers are taking a renewed look at SPACs as an IPO alternative. In a SPAC deal, a cash-poor private tech firm is acquired by a cashed-up public shell of a company. (SPAC stands for special purpose acquisition company). "SPACs are still alive," said Steven Halperin, co-head of capital solutions and head of public equity markets at Moelis & Co. "And as the IPO market gets more fickle and transaction sizes become larger and larger, will more companies think about going this route?" One reason why the SPAC route may be more appealing right now is a proposed regulatory change that could make it easier for newly public companies to raise new equity after their debut. One drawback of SPACs is that they don't guarantee a big infusion of cash, since investors in the SPAC can typically cash out their shares before the merger closes, which they often do if they don't like the business getting acquired. The Securities and Exchange Commission in May proposed easing restrictions on stock sales by newly public companies, including ones that go public via a SPAC. Among other changes, the proposal would eliminate a one-year waiting period for newly public companies to register for fast-tracked stock offerings. That could make it easier for those companies to take advantage of rallies in their share prices, including through ATMs and other deals already gaining traction with their public peers. items.title: In Private Funding, Like IPOs, Big Companies Dominate [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Shares of Anthropic fell below its $83 IPO price on Tuesday morning, summing up what has been a tough year for IPOs. While a couple of monster IPOs got done-Anthropic and SpaceX-only a handful of others made it through including offerings from SK Hynix, Cerebras and Lime. And as of Tuesday, all of those were trading below their IPO price. That makes it the fifth year in a row when the IPO market has been at least a bit disappointing. A bunch of companies are lined up for next year-including OpenAI-but slumping tech valuations fueled by skepticism about the AI boom clouds prospects for 2027. In that context, it's a decent time to take the pulse of startup dealmaking. One thing is clear: as in the IPO market this year, in the private fundraising market, the biggest companies are dominating. The top 10 private companies have more than doubled their combined valuation from $1.1 trillion to $2.6 trillion in just one year, Goldman's top tech banker Jane Dunlevie said on stage last week at Goldman Sachs' annual private tech conference in Las Vegas. She was talking about OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, Revolut, Anduril, Ramp, Cognition and Jeff Bezos's Prometheus. And more than half of those-OpenAI, Databricks, Anduril, Stripe, Ramp and Cognition-are now trying to raise billions more. There's still plenty of smaller startups emerging. Goldman managed to play matchmaker for more than 400 investors and 400-plus startups in the gilded corridors at the Encore Wynn Hotel. The mood was still electric, though investors are starting to think: as public market valuations fall, how should we value these private companies? One reason why private valuations can stay elevated even as public stocks drop is that venture investors tend to zoom in on growth. Many of these AI businesses' revenues have taken off, even as they bleed money thanks to expensive AI models they run and the chips they need to buy or rent. At a fireside chat at last week's confab, Winston Weinberg, CEO of legal AI startup Harvey, acknowledged that even with fast revenue growth, its gross margins fell to about negative 55% around June. They improved the figure by about 95% in roughly three months. Weinberg said annualized revenue grew from $190 million at the end of last year and expected to end this year with at least $675 million. "We're still early in the build out of AI, which means many of the defining companies of this era are not yet public and many investors are just getting to see the potential of those companies, both on growth and margin." Goldman's Jane Dunlevie said in an interview on the sidelines. She said each tech era has its own tests with investors: for internet companies, it was a path to profit; for subscription software firms, it was predictable revenue and net revenue retention. Meanwhile, attendees at the conference were staying hopeful about next year's IPO market. Some predicted that older venture-backed startups, such as Vercel, Ramp and Plaid, and even the older vertical software companies with some AI makeover, such as AlphaSense and Clio, will finally go public. In the two days of investors' schmoozing over fancy desserts and cocktails, a lineup of popular AI, chip and cybersecurity startups, like Legora, Unconventional AI and Abnormal AI fielded dozens of investors' meeting requests. Many older software startups were trying to remind investors they still exist. They are not getting too much love, say bankers and investors. One barometer of who's important in Las Vegas this year was whom Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon invited to his private dinner at the fancy restaurant Delilah. In attendance: Legora CEO Max Junestrand and Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao, said people familiar with the dinner. items.title: OpenAI Preps 'Athena' Data Tool to Make its Agents More Accurate [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: In its effort to win more business customers, OpenAI this fall launched an agent designed to help firms analyze their data and get answers to internal questions about their business. But at least one customer that has used the agent so far has found it isn't yet accurate enough for widespread use. That's a big problem. But OpenAI isn't sitting still. Representatives of the ChatGPT creator have told some customers and partners that they are developing a data management platform to help the agent perform better, according to the customer and three other people who spoke to OpenAI in recent weeks. The data management platform, code-named Athena, has similarities to what is known in the industry as a semantic layer, which companies use to create standardized definitions for business metrics such as revenue and customers, one of the people said. This type of software helps agents understand the difference between gross revenue and net revenue, or active and paying customers, the person added. One of the biggest reasons agents fail when companies use them with large amounts of complex business data is that they have to work out on their own what the data means and how it fits together, said Jason Strimpel, a managing director at Andersen Consulting who helps large companies use AI. "A semantic layer gives the agent that context from the start, often with plain-English descriptions of each item, so the agent has to guess less and [can work] faster and more accurately," he said.

(The full episode is available here.) Figuring out whether AI models have the kind of subjective experiences that constitute consciousness is quickly becoming a conundrum for the companies that train them. If they are conscious, and people fail to recognize that, mistreating them would be a moral catastrophe, said Long, who is the executive director of Eleos AI, a non-profit that researches AI consciousness and welfare. On the other hand, if people afford AI models undue moral consideration, that would hamstring developers' ability to crack down on rogue AI agents, he said.

items.content_text: If Jensen Huang was a tough taskmaster at Nvidia before, just imagine what he's going to be like now! His only problem is that he now owes his job to Trump. Just imagine what the newly restored CEO's relations with the president will be like in the future. What will Trump ask for in return? You know he'll want his pound of flesh. Will Trump ask Huang to give the government an equity stake in Nvidia? Trump has done that with other companies (in addition to asking for a cut of revenue from transactions in which government approval was needed). Or will the government ask to put people on Nvidia's board?
